source.title: The Generalization Error of Random Features Regression: Precise Asymptotics and the Double Descent Curve

record.tranche_reason: It derives and reports double-descent results for random-features ridge regression, a different method and model class from deep-network size sweeps; the model is equivalent to a two-layer network with a fixed random first layer.
record.gate_note: The paper reports its own asymptotic results and simulations on prediction error as width and sample size vary, and on regularization and error components. Related-work claims from other papers are not recorded as results. It also reports a coefficient-norm proxy for complexity; that finding is recorded separately because it does not test the versions' single-measure prediction across axes.
record.test_reason: The study derives exact asymptotic test error for random-features ridge regression and checks it by simulation, sweeping width, regularization and noise. Its own results bear on whether a double-descent curve appears outside deep networks (V4) and on its noise and regularization dependence (V6). It is not one of the original sources.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that random-features regression is an analytically tractable model that reproduces the full double-descent curve without ad hoc misspecification. Error diverges at N=n in both bias and variance, even at zero noise. Above the threshold error decreases monotonically, and the minimum is at extreme overparametrization. Optimal regularization removes the double descent, and above a critical SNR near-interpolators (λ→0) are optimal.
record.recipe_differences: The study derives high-dimensional asymptotics and runs simulations for ridge regression on random features, equivalent to a two-layer network with fixed random first-layer weights. It does not reproduce a deep-network training sweep.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported behavior varies with regularization (including optimized regularization), signal-to-noise ratio, activation, sample size, and whether the target includes nonlinear signal. The text says the peak becomes less prominent as regularization increases.

fits_no_version.finding: The penalty term ψ1‖â(λ)‖² rises up to the interpolation threshold, falls for N/n>1, and plateaus. The authors read this as model complexity decreasing past the threshold.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: A coefficient-norm complexity proxy is non-monotone in width and falls beyond interpolation in random-features regression.

record.peer_reviewed: Communications in Pure and Applied Mathematics
record.problems: The main results concern a random-features model with a fixed random first layer rather than fully trained deep networks. The sample-size sweep is reported only in a figure without a textual trend or recoverable values. Numerical illustrations use finite dimensions and averages over 20 instances; the asymptotic theory is stated for proportional limits.

untested.parts: Deep or fully trained networks are not studied; only a fixed-first-layer random-features model.
No sweep over epochs or training time. The ridge/early-stopping correspondence is only remarked, not tested.
Figure 2 (right) plots error against ψ2, but the text never states whether more data raises error near the threshold. The divergence at ψ1=ψ2 implies it, but the paper does not report it.
No single complexity measure is tested for predicting peak location across axes.
Triple or multiple descent is not studied.
Error is not re-plotted against an effective parameter count.

missing.what: Regularization sweep: the peak at N=n becomes less prominent as λ increases, and the lower envelope over λ is monotone decreasing. Shown at SNR ρ=5 and ρ=1/5.
With label noise (τ²=1, ψ2=2), the bias and variance curves both diverge at ψ1=ψ2 and both decrease above it.
Nonlinear targets at zero noise give nearly the same peaked curve as a linear target with noise: the nonlinear part acts like noise.
Ridgeless error against ψ1 with noise (ρ=2) for several ψ2 values. The global minimum is at ψ1→∞ for each.
In the wide limit, the optimal λ is 0 above a critical SNR ρ* and positive below it.

record.verdict_notes: The V1 links were moved to V4 because the system is not a deep network. V3 gets no verdict: Figure 2 (right) sweeps sample size, and Proposition 5.1's divergence at ψ1=ψ2 implies more data can hurt near the threshold, but the text never states this. The r8 complexity-proxy finding is close to the intuition behind V7, but error is not re-expressed against that proxy.

versions.untested_parts: The reported model is random-features regression, equivalent to a two-layer network with a fixed random first layer; fully trained or deeper networks are not tested.
No test-error sweep over training epochs or training time is reported. The stated connection between ridge regularization and early stopping is not an epoch-wise test.
A figure sweeps sample size, but the text does not state whether increasing data raises test error near the interpolation threshold, and the plotted values cannot be recovered from the supplied text.
The results cover random-features regression only, not a range of other model classes.
The paper measures a coefficient-norm proxy against width but does not test whether one effective-complexity measure predicts peak location across size, epochs, and sample count.
The paper does not test triple or multiple descent. It tests noiseless behavior and the effect of optimal regularization.
The paper does not re-express the curve against an effective parameter count to test whether it becomes an ordinary U-shaped curve.

rows.subject: random features ridge regression
rows.operation_detail: Analyzed asymptotic prediction error as the number of random features varies.
rows.measure: test (prediction) error; asymptotic bias and variance
rows.value: At ψ1 = ψ2, both bias and variance diverge; above the threshold, both are strictly decreasing in ψ1. In the small-width limit, bias tends to 1 and variance to 0.
rows.note: The text identifies ψ1 = ψ2 as the interpolation threshold and describes the curve as double descent. The model is a random-features, fixed-first-layer two-layer-network model, not a fully trained deep network.
rows.check: The model is random-features regression, a two-layer net whose fixed random first layer is never trained. That is not the deep-network system V1 names, so the row bears on V4 (other model classes), not V1.

conditions.value: λ = 10⁻⁸, used as a numerical approximation to λ → 0

rows.uncertainty: Standard error of the means over 20 instances is reported in the figure caption.
rows.note: The text says this figure displays the double-descent features and that, at zero noise, error is entirely due to bias. Numerical curve values are not stated.
rows.check: The V1 link is removed (not a deep network). For V6 the curve itself is observed, but it appears at zero noise (E[ε²]=0). That contradicts V6's claim that label noise drives the peak, so the row counts against that part of V6.

source_check.correct: V4: observed. V6 noise/variance-driven mechanism: absent; the double-descent peak persists without label noise and is entirely bias under the paper's decomposition.

rows.subject: random features ridge regression

rows.value: The bias has a peak at the interpolation threshold and diverges there when λ → 0; the paper also reports strict decrease above the threshold.
